questions.stem: According to the wounded Captain, what did Macbeth do to the rebel Macdonwald?
options: Captured him and sent him to Duncan for trial
Drove him back by sea to the Western Isles
Split him open and set his head on the battlements
Wounded him and let him flee to the Norwegian camp
questions.why: The Captain reports that Macbeth cut Macdonwald open "from the nave to the chops" and fixed his head on the battlements; the rebel was neither captured nor allowed to escape.

questions.stem: Speaking of the executed Thane of Cawdor, Duncan says, "There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face." Why is this line ironic as Macbeth enters right after it?
options: Duncan is about to trust another man whose looks hide treacherous thoughts
Duncan has already guessed that Macbeth wants the crown
Cawdor actually died without confessing any of his crimes
Macbeth has come to plead for Cawdor's life and title
questions.why: Duncan admits he was fooled by Cawdor and at once heaps trust on Macbeth, who in the same scene hides his "black and deep desires"; Malcolm reports that Cawdor did confess, so C is false.

questions.stem: Soon after Nick moves to West Egg, what makes him stop feeling lonely?
options: His Finnish housekeeper starts cooking his evening meals
A newcomer stops him on the road to ask the way to West Egg village
A young man from his office moves into the bungalow with him
Daisy telephones to invite him to dinner in East Egg
questions.why: Being asked for directions makes Nick feel like a settler; the coworker who found the house was sent to Washington, so Nick moved in alone.

questions.stem: Daisy repeats what she said after her daughter was born: "I hope she’ll be a fool—that’s the best thing a girl can be in this world, a beautiful little fool." What does the line suggest about Daisy's view of her world?
options: A girl will suffer less if she does not see too clearly how things are
She wishes her child had been born a boy instead
She is joking that her daughter already looks like Tom
She wants her daughter to grow up as sophisticated as herself
questions.why: Speaking from her own sense of abandonment, Daisy implies that knowing less would hurt less; she says she is glad it is a girl, so B is wrong.

questions.stem: According to Walton's first letter, what kept him from going to sea as a boy?
options: His sister Margaret's fear that he would drown on a voyage
His father's dying wish, which forbade his uncle to let him go
His uncle Thomas's own refusal to let him leave school
A weak constitution that left him unfit for hard labor
questions.why: B: the father's dying injunction bound the uncle; uncle Thomas only supplied the books of voyages, so C reverses who forbade it.

questions.stem: When Walton says he would sacrifice everything to his enterprise, the stranger cries, "Do you share my madness? Have you drank also of the intoxicating draught?" What does the image of the draught suggest?
options: Walton has been drinking with the crew to keep up his spirits
Walton's thirst for discovery is a dangerous craving the stranger once gave in to
The stranger blames the brandy the sailors forced him to swallow
The stranger envies Walton's hope and wishes to share it
questions.why: B: the 'draught' is Walton's ambition, which the stranger calls a shared 'madness' and urges him to 'dash the cup' away; the brandy in C is a literal detail, not the meaning.

questions.stem: When Edna comes back from the beach, what does Mr. Pontellier take from his vest pocket and hand to her?
options: The rings she had left with him before bathing
A ten-dollar bill to spend on the children's treats
A letter from her sister who is away in the East
The key to the family's bath-house on the beach
questions.why: Edna silently reaches out and he returns her rings; the ten-dollar bill stays in his pocket for the game at Klein's.

questions.stem: After the ladies praise the box of treats from New Orleans, the narrator adds: "Mrs. Pontellier was forced to admit that she knew of none better." What does the word "forced" suggest?
options: Her husband ordered her to praise him.
She is jealous that the other ladies admire her husband.
She is embarrassed that the box is smaller than usual.
She agrees under pressure, without real warmth.
questions.why: Coming right after the scene of the night before, "forced" shows Edna conceding the point because the facts and the company require it, not out of feeling.
